title: 3Sum
problem: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] taken from different indices such that a + b + c == 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triplets (order inside the result does not matter).
example: Explanation: -1 + -1 + 2 = 0 and -1 + 0 + 1 = 0. No other distinct triplet sums to 0.
intuition: If we fix one number a, the problem becomes "find pairs b + c = -a " in the rest of the array. That is Two Sum. If the array is sorted, Two Sum on a sorted array is a classic two-pointer walk: if the sum is too small move the left pointer right, if too big move the right pointer left.

Sorting also solves the harder part of this problem: duplicates. In a sorted array equal values sit next to each other, so we can skip a value if it equals the previous one, both for the fixed element and for the two pointers after a match. That gives unique triplets without a Set.
Trace on sorted [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]: fix -4, need 4, best pair is 1+2=3, none. Fix -1 (index 1), need 1: -1+2=1 match, then 0+1=1 match. Fix -1 (index 2): same value as before, skip. Done.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force checks all triplets in O(n³) and dedupes with a set. Sorting lets me fix one number and run a two-pointer Two Sum on the rest, which is O(n²) with O(1) extra space, and because equal values are adjacent I can skip duplicates without any set."
Edge cases: fewer than 3 elements; all zeros [0,0,0,0] (answer is one triplet); all positive or all negative (empty answer).
Common mistakes: forgetting to skip duplicates for both i and lo; in JS using nums.sort() without a comparator (sorts as strings, so -4 and 10 go wrong).

Follow-ups: "3Sum Closest?" Same loop, track the sum with the smallest |sum - target|. "4Sum?" Add one more fixed loop (see 2.8). "Can you do it without sorting?" Yes with the hashing approach, but dedupe needs a set and extra space. 2.2
simple: Find all different groups of three numbers that add to zero.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Try every triplet i < j < k.
If the sum is 0, sort the triplet and put it into a set to remove duplicates.
Return the set as a list.
approaches.why: Three nested loops dominate; the set insert costs a log factor (or hashing), and m is the number of unique triplets stored.
approaches.simple: Try every triple, keep the ones summing to zero, and use a set to throw away duplicates.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Fix i. For every j > i, the needed third value is -(nums[i] + nums[j]).
Keep a hash set of values seen between i and j; if the needed value is in it, we found a triplet.
Sort the triplet and add to a global set to dedupe.
approaches.why: Two loops with O(1) hash lookups; the inner set holds up to n values and the result set holds m triplets.
approaches.simple: Fix the first number, then do a Two Sum with a hash set for the other two.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort nums.
For each i, skip it if nums[i] == nums[i-1] (same fixed value already handled). If nums[i] > 0 you can stop: everything after is positive too.
Set lo = i + 1, hi = n - 1. While lo < hi: if sum < 0 move lo++; if sum > 0 move hi--; if sum == 0 record it, move both, and skip duplicates of nums[lo].
approaches.space: O(1) extra (ignoring output and sort's internal stack)
approaches.why: Sorting is O(n log n); for each of n fixed values the two-pointer scan is O(n).
approaches.simple: Sort. Fix the first number, then squeeze two pointers from both ends of the rest. Skip equal values so each triple appears once.

title: Container With Most Water
problem: height[i] is the height of a vertical line at position i. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container. Return the maximum amount of water a container can hold. Area = min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i).
example: Explanation: Lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7): min(8, 7) * (8 - 1) = 49.
intuition: Start with the widest container: l = 0, r = n - 1. Now we must shrink the width. Which side do we move? The water level is limited by the shorter line. If we move the taller line inward, the width drops and the height can never go above the shorter line, so the area can only get worse. So any container that uses the shorter line with a smaller width is useless: we can drop the shorter line for good and move its pointer inward.
That is the key two-pointer argument: every step safely eliminates one line, so we check only n containers instead of n²/2.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force checks all pairs in O(n²). With two pointers at the ends, the shorter line limits the area, and moving the taller one can only shrink width without raising the height, so I always move the shorter one. That gives O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: two lines only; all equal heights; zeros in the array.
Common mistakes: moving the taller pointer; confusing this with Trapping Rain Water (here only two lines matter, the lines in between are ignored).
Follow-ups: "Prove the greedy is correct?" Any pair using the shorter line with a smaller width has area ≤ current area, so discarding that line loses nothing. 2.3
simple: Pick two vertical lines that, with the floor, hold the most water.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Try every pair i < j.
Compute min(h[i], h[j]) * (j - i) and keep the max.
approaches.why: Every pair is checked once with constant work.
approaches.simple: Try every pair of lines and compute the water each pair holds.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: l = 0, r = n - 1, best = 0.
Compute the area for (l, r) and update best.
Move the pointer at the shorter line inward (if equal, move either).
Repeat until l == r.
approaches.why: Each step moves one pointer inward, so at most n - 1 steps.
approaches.simple: Start with the widest pair. The shorter line limits the water, so move that one inward; moving the taller one can never help.

title: Trapping Rain Water
problem: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where each bar has width 1, compute how much rain water is trapped after raining.
example: Explanation: Water sits in the dips: 1 unit at index 2, 1 at 4, 2 at 5, 1 at 6, 1 at 9.
intuition: Think about one column i at a time. Water above it rises up to the level of the shorter of the two "walls": the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right. So water[i] = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) - height[i] (never negative, since the max includes height[i] itself).

The brute force recomputes maxLeft and maxRight for each i. Precomputing them in two arrays makes it O(n). The final trick removes the arrays: keep two pointers and the running leftMax and rightMax. If leftMax < rightMax, then for the left pointer the binding wall is definitely leftMax (the right side has something at least rightMax, which is bigger). So we can settle the left column now and move left. Otherwise settle the right column.
notes: Say it like this: "Water at each index is min(max on left, max on right) minus its height. Brute force recomputes those maxima per index in O(n²); prefix and suffix max arrays make it O(n) time and O(n) space; and two pointers bring space down to O(1), because whichever side has the smaller bar is the side whose max is the binding wall."
Edge cases: empty array or fewer than 3 bars (answer 0); strictly increasing or decreasing heights (0); a flat array.
Common mistakes: comparing leftMax vs rightMax but then updating the wrong pointer; forgetting to update the max before adding (then you can get negative water).

Follow-ups: "Monotonic stack solution?" Yes: keep a decreasing stack of indices, when a taller bar comes, pop and add water bounded between the new bar and the new stack top, O(n) time and O(n) space. "2D version (Trapping Rain Water II)?" Use a min-heap from the borders inward (BFS with priority queue). 2.4
simple: Bars of different heights stand in a row. After rain, how much water sits between them?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each index i, scan left to find the max bar and scan right to find the max bar.
Add min(leftMax, rightMax) - height[i].
approaches.why: For each of n columns we scan the whole array.
approaches.simple: For each bar, look left for the tallest bar and right for the tallest bar. Water above this bar is the smaller of the two minus its own height.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Build prefixMax[i] = max of height[0..i] in one left-to-right pass.
Build suffixMax[i] = max of height[i..n-1] in one right-to-left pass.
Sum min(prefixMax[i], suffixMax[i]) - height[i].
approaches.why: Three linear passes; two extra arrays of size n.
approaches.simple: Pre-compute the tallest bar to the left and to the right of every spot in two passes, then add up the water.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: l = 0, r = n - 1, leftMax = rightMax = 0.
While l < r: if height[l] < height[r], the left side is the bottleneck. Update leftMax, add leftMax - height[l], move l++.
Otherwise do the same on the right: update rightMax, add rightMax - height[r], move r--.
approaches.why: One pass with two pointers meeting in the middle; only four variables.
approaches.simple: Two pointers from both ends. The side with the lower wall decides the water level there, so handle that side and move it inward.

title: Two Sum II Input Array Is Sorted
problem: Given a 1-indexed array numbers sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers that add up to target and return their indices [index1, index2] (1-based, index1 < index2). Exactly one solution exists, and you must use only constant extra space.
intuition: Because the array is sorted, the smallest possible sum uses the leftmost element and the largest uses the rightmost. Put l at the start and r at the end. If numbers[l] + numbers[r] is too small, the only way to increase it is to move l right (moving r left would only make it smaller). If it is too big, move r left. Each step rules out one element for good.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force is O(n²). Binary searching the complement gives O(n log n). Since the array is sorted, two pointers from both ends give O(n) time and O(1) space: too small means move left up, too big means move right down."
Edge cases: negative numbers; duplicate values like [3,3], target 6; answer at the two ends.
Common mistakes: returning 0-based indices; using a HashMap (works, but breaks the O(1) space requirement).
Follow-ups: "What if not sorted?" Use a HashMap, O(n) time and O(n) space (Two Sum I), or sort with indices for O(n log n). 2.5
simple: The list is sorted. Find two numbers that add to the target (answer is 1-based).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Try every pair i < j.
Return [i+1, j+1] when the sum equals target.
approaches.why: All pairs are checked in the worst case.
approaches.simple: Try every pair.

approaches.label: Better
steps: For each i, binary search the range i+1..n-1 for target - numbers[i].
Return the pair when found.
approaches.why: n binary searches of O(log n) each.
approaches.simple: For each number, binary search the rest of the sorted list for its partner.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: While l < r: compute sum. If equal to target, return [l+1, r+1]. If smaller, l++. If larger, r--.
approaches.why: Each step moves one pointer; they meet after at most n steps.
approaches.simple: One finger at each end. Sum too small? Move left finger right. Too big? Move right finger left.

title: Valid Palindrome
problem: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome.
example: Input:    s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
Explanation: Cleaned string is "amanaplanacanalpanama", which reads the same both ways.
intuition: The simple way is to build the cleaned string and compare it to its reverse. But we do not need a new string: put one pointer at each end, skip characters that are not letters or digits, and compare the lowercase versions. If any pair differs, it is not a palindrome.
notes: Say it like this: "The simple version cleans the string and compares it to its reverse, O(n) time and O(n) space. With two pointers that skip non-alphanumeric characters and compare in lowercase, I get the same O(n) time with O(1) space."
Edge cases: empty string or only punctuation like " " or ".," (true); digits like "0P" (false, digits count).
Common mistakes: forgetting l < r in the inner skip loops (index out of bounds); ignoring digits.
Follow-ups: "Valid Palindrome II: can delete at most one char?" On the first mismatch, check if s[l+1..r] or s[l..r-1] is a palindrome, still O(n). 2.6
simple: Ignoring case and anything that is not a letter or digit, does the text read the same forwards and backwards?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Build a cleaned lowercase string of only letters and digits.
Compare it with its reverse.
approaches.why: One pass to clean, one to reverse; the cleaned copy and its reverse take O(n).
approaches.simple: Make a clean lowercase copy with only letters and digits, then compare it with its reverse.

f.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

e.a: s="A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

f.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Move l forward while s[l] is not alphanumeric; move r backward likewise.
Compare lowercase s[l] and s[r]; if different return false; else l++, r--.
approaches.why: Each character is visited at most once by one of the pointers; no copy is made.
approaches.simple: Two pointers from both ends, skipping junk characters, comparing letters as they meet in the middle.

title: Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's
problem: Given an array nums with values only 0, 1 and 2 (red, white, blue), sort it in place so that all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s. Do not use the library sort (LeetCode 75, "Sort Colors").
example: Explanation: Two 0s, two 1s and two 2s in order.
intuition: Any sort works but is O(n log n). Since there are only three values, we can count them and rewrite the array: O(n) but two passes. The one-pass trick (Dutch National Flag) keeps three regions while scanning: - [0, low-1] all 0s, [low, mid-1] all 1s, [mid, high] unknown, [high+1, n-1] all 2s.

Look at nums[mid]: if 0, swap it into the 0 region (low++, mid++); if 1, it is already in place (mid++); if 2, swap it to the end (high--) but do not move mid, because the element swapped in from high is still unknown.
notes: Say it like this: "Library sort is O(n log n). Counting is O(n) but two passes. The Dutch National Flag algorithm does it in one pass with O(1) space using low, mid and high pointers, sending 0s to the front and 2s to the back."
Edge cases: all same value; already sorted; length 1.
Common mistakes: incrementing mid after swapping with high (the swapped-in value is unchecked); using mid < high instead of mid <= high.

Follow-ups: "Why can we move mid after swapping with low?" The value coming from low is always 1 (or it is the same element), since everything between low and mid is already 1s. "k colors?" Counting sort, O(n + k). 2.7
simple: Sort a list that only has 0s, 1s and 2s.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Sort the array with the library sort.
approaches.why: Comparison sort cost; Java's dual-pivot quicksort uses recursion stack.
approaches.simple: Just use the built-in sort.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Count how many 0s, 1s and 2s there are.
Overwrite the array: c0 zeros, then c1 ones, then c2 twos.
approaches.why: Two passes over the array; three counters.
approaches.simple: Count the 0s, 1s and 2s, then rewrite the list with that many of each.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: low = 0, mid = 0, high = n - 1.
While mid <= high: - nums[mid] == 0: swap with nums[low], low++, mid++. - nums[mid] == 1: mid++. - nums[mid] == 2: swap with nums[high], high-- (do not move mid).
approaches.why: Every step either moves mid forward or high backward, so at most n steps, in one pass.
approaches.simple: Dutch flag: three pointers. 0s get swapped to the front, 2s to the back, 1s stay in the middle. One pass.

title: Next Permutation
pattern: Array scan from the right + reverse
problem: Rearrange nums in place into the lexicographically next greater permutation. If no greater one exists (the array is in descending order), rearrange it into the lowest possible order (ascending). Use only constant extra memory.
example: Explanation: Permutations in order: 123, 132, 213, ... The one after 123 is 132.
intuition: Think of the number like an odometer. To get the next bigger number, we want to change the rightmost possible position by the smallest possible amount. Scan from the right: the suffix that is in decreasing order is already at its maximum, nothing can be done inside it. The first index i from the right where nums[i] < nums[i+1] is the "pivot", the place we must bump up.

Swap the pivot with the smallest value in the suffix that is bigger than it (scan from the right, the first one bigger than nums[i]). The suffix is still decreasing after the swap, so reverse it to make it the smallest (ascending). Example: [1, 3, 5, 4, 2] → pivot is 3 (index 1), smallest bigger in suffix [5,4,2] is 4, swap → [1, 4, 5, 3, 2], reverse suffix → [1, 4, 2, 3, 5].
If no pivot exists, the whole array is decreasing: just reverse it.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force lists all n! permutations and picks the next one, which is hopeless. The optimal way finds the first dip from the right, swaps it with the next larger element in the suffix, and reverses the suffix. That is O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: fully descending [3,2,1] → [1,2,3]; duplicates like [1,5,1] → [5,1,1] (use >= and <= in the scans); single element.
Common mistakes: sorting the suffix instead of reversing (works but O(n log n)); using strict > in the pivot scan, which breaks on duplicates.

Follow-ups: "Previous permutation?" Mirror it: find first i from the right with nums[i] > nums[i+1], swap with largest smaller value in the suffix, reverse. "k-th permutation?" Use factorial number system (LeetCode 60). 2.8
simple: Rearrange the numbers into the very next bigger arrangement (like the next word in a dictionary).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Generate all distinct permutations with recursion and keep them in sorted (lexicographic) order.
Find the current one, return the next (or the first if it was the last).
approaches.why: There are n! permutations, each of length n, and we store them all. Only feasible for tiny n; mention it, do not code it in an interview unless asked.
approaches.simple: List every arrangement in sorted order, find the current one, and take the next.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Find the largest i with nums[i] < nums[i+1] (scan from the right). If none, reverse the whole array and stop.
Find the largest j > i with nums[j] > nums[i] (scan from the right). Swap nums[i] and nums[j].
Reverse nums[i+1..n-1].
approaches.why: At most three linear scans (find pivot, find successor, reverse), all in place.
approaches.simple: From the right, find the first number smaller than its right neighbour. Swap it with the smallest bigger number to its right, then reverse the tail.

title: 4 Sum
problem: Given an array nums and an integer target, return all unique quadruplets [a, b, c, d] from distinct indices such that a + b + c + d == target.
example: Explanation: These are the only distinct sets of four numbers summing to 0.
intuition: This is 3Sum with one more loop. Sort the array, fix the first two numbers with two loops, and find the last two with the two-pointer walk. Skip duplicates at every level, exactly like 3Sum.
One trap: values go up to 10⁹, so the sum of four can overflow int. Use long for the sum in Java.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force is four loops, O(n⁴). Hashing the last element gives O(n³) but needs a set to dedupe. Sorting and fixing two elements, then running two pointers, is O(n³) with O(1) extra space and dedupes naturally by skipping equal neighbours."
Edge cases: fewer than 4 elements; large values like [1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000] with target -294967296 (int overflow would give a false match); many duplicates.
Common mistakes: int overflow in Java; skipping duplicate j with j > 0 instead of j > i + 1 (wrongly skips valid quadruplets).
Follow-ups: "k-Sum in general?" Recursion that reduces k-Sum to (k-1)-Sum until 2Sum with two pointers, O(n^(k-1)). 2.9
simple: Find all different groups of four numbers that add to the target.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Four nested loops over i < j < k < l.
If the sum (as long) equals target, sort the quadruplet and add to a set.
approaches.why: Four loops; m unique quadruplets stored in the set.
approaches.simple: Try every group of four and remove duplicates with a set.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Fix i and j. For each k > j, the needed fourth value is target - (nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k]).
Look it up in a hash set of values seen between j and k.
Sort found quadruplets and dedupe with a set.
approaches.why: Three loops with O(1) lookups; the inner hash set and the result set.
approaches.simple: Fix two numbers, and use a hash set to find the other two.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Sort nums.
Loop i, skip duplicates. Loop j > i, skip duplicates (j > i + 1 && nums[j] == nums[j-1]).
Two pointers lo = j + 1, hi = n - 1; compare the long sum with target and move like 3Sum, skipping duplicates after each match.
approaches.why: Two fixed loops times a linear two-pointer scan; sorting O(n log n) is dominated.
approaches.simple: Sort. Fix two numbers with two loops, then squeeze two pointers for the last two, skipping duplicates.

title: Merge two sorted arrays without extra space
pattern: Two pointers / Gap method (Shell sort idea)
problem: You are given two sorted arrays a (size n) and b (size m). Merge them so that, after the operation, a holds the smallest n elements and b holds the remaining m elements, both in sorted order. You may not use an extra array; modify a and b in place. (This is the GFG/Striver version. LeetCode 88 "Merge Sorted Array" is a simpler cousin, covered in the follow-ups.)
example: Explanation: Merged order is 1 2 3 4 8 9 10; first 4 go to a, the rest to b.
intuition: With an extra array this is plain merge sort's merge step. Without it, notice one fact: the smallest n elements must end up in a. Compare the largest of a (from its end) with the smallest of b (from its start). While a[i] > b[j], those two are in the wrong arrays, so swap them and move inward. Once a[i] <= b[j], everything is in the right array. Each array may now be unsorted, so sort both. That is the "better" approach.

The optimal one is the gap method, borrowed from Shell sort. Treat a followed by b as one virtual array of length n + m. Start with gap = ceil((n+m)/2), compare elements gap apart and swap if out of order, then shrink the gap (ceil(gap/2)) until it is 1. After the gap-1 pass the whole virtual array is sorted.
notes: Say it like this: "With extra space it is a simple O(n+m) merge. Without extra space, I can swap a's largest with b's smallest while they are out of order and then sort both, O(n log n + m log m). The gap method from Shell sort does it in O((n+m) log(n+m)) with O(1) space by treating both arrays as one."
Edge cases: one array empty; all of a smaller than all of b (no swaps); all of a bigger than all of b (full swap).
Common mistakes: using floor instead of ceil for the gap (you can skip the gap-1 pass); forgetting to stop after the gap-1 pass (infinite loop since ceil(1/2) = 1).

Follow-ups: "LeetCode 88: nums1 has size m + n with trailing zeros?" Fill from the back: three pointers i = m- 1, j = n-1, k = m+n-1, put the larger of nums1[i] and nums2[j] at k. O(m + n) time and O(1) space, because the empty tail of nums1 is free space. 2.10
simple: Two sorted lists. Merge them so the first list holds the smallest numbers and the second the rest, without a big extra array.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Merge both into a temp array of size n + m using two pointers.
Copy the first n back into a, the rest into b.
approaches.why: One linear merge plus a copy; uses the temp array (breaks the rule, but is the baseline).
approaches.simple: Merge both into a temporary list, then copy the pieces back.

approaches.label: Better
steps: i = n - 1 (end of a), j = 0 (start of b).
While i >= 0 && j < m && a[i] > b[j]: swap a[i] and b[j], i--, j++.
Sort a and sort b.
approaches.time: O(min(n, m) + n log n + m log m)
approaches.why: The swap loop runs at most min(n, m) times; then two sorts.
approaches.simple: Swap the biggest items of the first list with the smallest of the second while they are out of order, then sort each list.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: len = n + m, gap = ceil(len / 2).
For left = 0, right = gap while right < len: get the elements at virtual positions left and right (position p < n is a[p], else b[p - n]); if the left one is bigger, swap. Move both forward.
If gap == 1 stop, else gap = ceil(gap / 2) and repeat.
approaches.why: About log(n + m) gap values, each pass is linear; swaps are in place.
approaches.simple: Gap method: compare items a gap apart across both lists and swap if out of order, shrinking the gap by half each round.

title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock
problem: prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximize profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.
example: Explanation: Buy on day 1 (price 1), sell on day 4 (price 6), profit 6 - 1 = 5.
intuition: If you sell on day i, the best buy day is the cheapest day before i. So walk left to right, keep the minimum price seen so far, and at each day check price - minSoFar. As a window: left is the buy day (the minimum so far) and right is the sell day; whenever prices[right] < prices[left], jump left to right, since a cheaper buy day makes every future sale better.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force checks every buy/sell pair in O(n²). For each sell day the best buy is the minimum before it, so I track the running minimum in one pass: O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: strictly decreasing prices (answer 0); single day; all equal.
Common mistakes: finding global min and global max separately (the max may come before the min); returning a negative profit.
Follow-ups: "Unlimited transactions (Stock II)?" Sum every positive day-to-day difference. "At most two / k transactions, cooldown, fee?" These become DP with buy/sell states. Longest Substring 2.11
simple: Buy once, sell later. What is the biggest profit?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every buy day i and every later sell day j, compute prices[j] - prices[i].
Keep the max (start at 0).
approaches.why: All pairs of days are checked.
approaches.simple: Try every buy day with every later sell day.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: minPrice = +infinity, best = 0.
For each price: update minPrice = min(minPrice, price), then best = max(best, price - minPrice).
approaches.why: One pass with two variables.
approaches.simple: Walk through the days remembering the cheapest price so far. Each day, check the profit if you sold today.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problem: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring (contiguous) with no repeating characters.
example: Explanation: "abc" is the longest substring without a repeat; length 3.
intuition: A window [left, right] is valid if all its characters are distinct. Expand right one character at a time. If the new character already exists inside the window, the window is invalid, and any window that still contains the old copy is invalid too, so move left just past the old copy. Every valid window gives a candidate length right - left + 1.

Store the last index of each character. Then on a repeat we can jump left directly to lastIndex + 1 instead of stepping one by one. Only jump forward: left = max(left, last[c] + 1), because the old copy may already be outside the window.
Trace "abba": a(l=0), b(l=0), b repeats at 1 → l=2, a was at 0, but max(2, 1) keeps l=2. Best = 2.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries every start and extends while unique, O(n²). A sliding window with a set is O(n) since each char enters and leaves once. Storing last seen indices lets left jump directly past the repeat, still O(n) but a single pass, with O(alphabet) space."
Edge cases: empty string (0); all same "bbbb" (1); spaces and symbols (they count as characters); "abba" (left must not move backward).
Common mistakes: moving left backward by not checking last[c] >= left; using int[26] when input has digits/spaces.
Follow-ups: "Return the substring itself?" Track the start index when best updates. "At most K distinct characters?" See 2.18. 2.12
simple: Find the longest stretch of text with no repeated letter.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i, extend j while characters stay unique (use a set).
Track the longest length.
approaches.why: Each start extends up to n characters; σ is the alphabet size held in the set.
approaches.simple: From each start, grow until a letter repeats, and track the longest.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Sliding window with a set: expand right.
While s[right] is in the set, remove s[left] and left++.
Add s[right], update best.
approaches.why: Each character is added once and removed at most once (2n operations).
approaches.simple: Sliding window with a set. Grow on the right; if the new letter is already inside, drop letters from the left until it isn't.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep last[c] = last index where character c appeared (array of 128 or a map).
For each right: if c was seen, left = max(left, last[c] + 1).
Set last[c] = right, update best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.why: Exactly one pass, left jumps without inner loops; the index table is alphabet-sized.
approaches.simple: Remember the last place each letter was seen. When a letter repeats, jump the left edge straight past its last position.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problem: Given an uppercase string s and an integer k, you may change at most k characters to any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring containing only one repeated letter you can get.
example: Explanation: Change the 'A' at index 3 to 'B' to get "AABBBBA"; "BBBB" has length 4.
intuition: For a fixed window, the best plan is to keep the most frequent letter and replace the rest. The number of replacements needed is windowLength - maxFreq. The window is valid when that is <= k.
So use the template: expand right, update counts and maxFreq; while len - maxFreq > k, shrink from the left. Record the length.

A neat optimization: we never need to decrease maxFreq when shrinking. The answer only improves when we find a window with a bigger maxFreq, so a stale (too high) maxFreq just means the window does not grow; it never produces a wrong larger answer. With that, the window never shrinks by more than one per step, and if replaces while.
notes: Say it like this: "A window is valid if its length minus its most frequent letter count is at most k. Brute force checks every start in O(n²). A sliding window that recomputes the max is O(26n), and since the answer only grows when maxFreq grows, I can keep a stale maxFreq and get O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: k = 0 (longest run of one letter); k >= n (whole string); single character.
Common mistakes: thinking the stale maxFreq is a bug and "fixing" it wrongly; using while with stale maxFreq (still correct, but understand why if is enough).
Follow-ups: "Binary string, flip at most k zeros?" That is Max Consecutive Ones III (2.17), same idea. 2.13
simple: You may change up to k letters. What is the longest stretch you can make of one repeated letter?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i, extend j and keep a frequency array and the max frequency.
If (j - i + 1) - maxFreq <= k, update best; else break (longer windows from i only need more changes).
approaches.why: n starts, each extending up to n; fixed-size count array.
approaches.simple: From each start, grow while (length − count of the most common letter) is at most k.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Sliding window: expand right, increment its count.
While len - (max over 26 counts) > k, decrement s[left] and left++ (recompute the true max each time).
Update best.
approaches.why: Each step may scan 26 counts to get the true maximum.
approaches.simple: Sliding window. If the window needs more than k changes, shrink it from the left. Recount the most common letter each time.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Expand right, update cnt and maxFreq = max(maxFreq, cnt[c]).
If len - maxFreq > k, move left one step (decrement its count). Do not recompute maxFreq.
best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.why: Constant work per character; maxFreq is never recomputed.
approaches.simple: Same window, but keep the best most-common count seen so far instead of recounting. The window never shrinks below the best answer, so it still works.

title: Permutation In String
problem: Given strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1 as a substring. In other words, some window of s2 of length |s1| is an anagram of s1. Both strings are lowercase letters.
example: Explanation: s2 contains "ba", which is a permutation of "ab".
intuition: A permutation has the same length and the same letter counts. So slide a window of exactly |s1| across s2 and compare counts. Instead of rebuilding counts for each window, add the entering char and remove the leaving char: O(1) update.

Comparing two 26-length arrays each step is O(26), which is fine. For a true O(n), keep a counter matches = number of letters (out of 26) whose counts are equal in both, and update it only for the two letters that changed.
notes: Say it like this: "A permutation means same length and same counts, so I slide a fixed window of size |s1| over s2. Sorting each window is O(n·m log m). Keeping two count arrays and comparing is O(26n), and tracking how many of the 26 letters match makes it O(n) with O(1) space."
Edge cases: s1 longer than s2 (false); match at the very end (check after the loop); s1 of length 1.
Common mistakes: forgetting the final check after the loop; updating matches before updating the count.
Follow-ups: "Return all start indices?" That is Find All Anagrams in a String (LeetCode 438), same window, collect indices. 2.14
simple: Does the second string contain a rearrangement of the first as a continuous piece?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every window start i in s2 of length |s1|, sort the window and compare with sorted s1.
approaches.why: n - m + 1 windows, each sorted; m = |s1|, n = |s2|.
approaches.simple: Check every window of the right size by sorting it and comparing with the sorted first string.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Count letters of s1 into need[26], and the first window of s2 into win[26].
Slide: compare arrays; then add s2[i], remove s2[i - m].
approaches.why: Each slide is O(1), each comparison is O(26).
approaches.simple: Slide a window of letter counts across the string and compare its 26 counts with the target counts.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Build need and the first window win; compute matches = number of letters c with need[c] == win[c].
If matches == 26 return true.
Slide: for the entering letter, update win, then adjust matches (if it became equal, +1; if it was equal and now is not, -1). Same for the leaving letter. Check matches == 26.
approaches.why: O(26) setup, then constant work per slide.
approaches.simple: Slide the window and keep a single number: how many of the 26 letters currently have matching counts. When all 26 match, you found it.

title: Minimum Window Substring
problem: Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (including duplicates). If none exists, return "". The answer is unique when it exists.
example: Explanation: "BANC" contains A, B and C, and no shorter window does.
intuition: This is the "minimum" flavour of the window template: expand right until the window is valid (it covers t), then shrink left as much as possible while it stays valid, recording the smallest size. When it breaks, go back to expanding.

To check "valid" in O(1), keep need[c] = count of c in t, and missing = total characters of t still not covered. When s[right] enters and need[c] > 0, it is useful, so missing--; then need[c]-- (it can go negative, meaning extra copies). When s[left] leaves, need[c]++; if it becomes > 0, we just lost a needed char, so missing++. The window is valid when missing == 0.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries each start and extends until the window covers t, O(n²). The sliding window expands right until valid, then shrinks left while still valid to find the minimum. A single 'missing' counter makes the validity check O(1), so total time is O(|s| + |t|) and space is O(alphabet)."
Edge cases: t longer than s (""); t has duplicates like "AA"; no valid window; s == t.

Common mistakes: counting only distinct characters of t and ignoring duplicates; recording the answer after shrinking instead of before; building substrings inside the loop (store start and length instead).
Follow-ups: "Unicode / large alphabet?" Use a HashMap instead of an array. "Minimum window subsequence (order matters)?" Different problem, DP or two-pass scan. 2.15
simple: Find the shortest piece of s that contains every letter of t (with repeats).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i, extend j, maintaining counts of s[i..j].
As soon as the window covers t, record its length and stop extending (longer is never better for this i).
approaches.time: O(n²) (O(n² · σ) if you compare full count arrays instead of a counter)
approaches.why: n starts each extending up to n; counts are alphabet-sized.
approaches.simple: From each start, grow until all needed letters are covered and remember the shortest.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Fill need[] from t; missing = |t|; left = 0.
For each right: if need[s[right]] > 0, missing--; then need[s[right]]--.
While missing == 0: record window if smaller; then need[s[left]]++; if it becomes > 0, missing++; left++.
Return the best window or "".
approaches.why: right and left each move at most |s| times; σ = 128 for ASCII.
approaches.simple: Sliding window. Grow right until nothing is missing, then shrink from the left as long as it still covers t, recording the shortest window.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
problem: Given an array nums and window size k, a window slides from left to right one step at a time. Return an array of the maximum value in each window.
intuition: The hard part is removing the leaving element: a running max cannot "un-include" a value. Observation: if a newer element is bigger than an older one, the older one can never be a window max again (the newer one outlives it and beats it). So we only need to keep candidates in decreasing order of value.

Use a deque of indices, values decreasing from front to back. For each new index i: pop from the back while the back value <= nums[i] (they are useless now); push i; pop from the front if its index fell out of the window (<= i - k). The front is always the max of the current window.
A middle option is a max-heap of (value, index), lazily discarding tops that are out of the window: O(n log n).
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force scans each window, O(n·k). A max-heap with lazy deletion is O(n log n). A monotonic decreasing deque of indices keeps only elements that can still become a max, giving O(n) time and O(k) space, since each index enters and leaves once."
Edge cases: k == 1 (answer is the array); k == n (one value); duplicates (pop with <= or <, both work, <= keeps the deque smaller); negatives.
Common mistakes: storing values instead of indices (then you cannot tell when the front expired); using Array.shift() in JS (O(n) per call).
Follow-ups: "Sliding window minimum?" Same with an increasing deque. "Median of each window?" Two heaps or an ordered multiset, O(n log k). 2.16
simple: For each window of k neighbours, report the biggest number.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each window start i from 0 to n - k, scan the k elements for the max.
approaches.why: n - k + 1 windows, each scanned in O(k).
approaches.simple: For every window, scan its k numbers for the max.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Push [value, index] into a max-heap as right moves.
While the heap top's index is outside the window, poll it (lazy deletion).
Once right >= k - 1, the top is the window max.
approaches.why: Each element is pushed and popped once at O(log n); stale entries can pile up to n.
approaches.simple: Keep a max-heap of numbers in view; throw away the top if it has slid out of the window.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Deque dq of indices with decreasing values.
For each i: if dq.front <= i - k, pop front. While nums[dq.back] <= nums[i], pop back. Push i at back.
If i >= k - 1, append nums[dq.front] to the answer.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once; the deque never holds more than k indices.
approaches.simple: Keep a queue of positions with decreasing values. New numbers knock out smaller ones from the back; the front is always the window's max.

title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
problem: Cards are in a row with points cardPoints[i]. In one step you take a card from either the beginning or the end of the row. You must take exactly k cards. Return the maximum total points.
example: Explanation: Take the last three cards 5 + 6 + 1 = 12, which beats any other mix of front and back.
intuition: Whatever order you pick, you end up with some i cards from the front and k - i cards from the back, for i from 0 to k. So there are only k + 1 possible outcomes. Start with all k from the front, then repeatedly swap the last front card for the next back card: this is a window that "wraps around" and slides by one, updated in O(1).
Equivalent view: the cards you do not take form a contiguous middle block of size n - k. Maximizing what you take = total minus the minimum-sum window of size n - k. Both views are O(n) or O(k).
notes: Say it like this: "Any valid pick is i cards from the front and k minus i from the back, so there are only k + 1 options. Summing each directly is O(k²); sliding from 'all front' to 'all back' updates the sum in O(1) per step, so O(k) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: k == n (take everything); k == 1; all equal values.

Common mistakes: picking greedily (the bigger end each time). Counterexample: [2, 100, 1, 1, 3], k = 2: greedy takes 3 then 2 = 5, but taking 2 and 100 from the front gives 102. Enumerate the k + 1 splits instead.
Follow-ups: "Explain the complement view?" Minimize a size n - k contiguous window; answer is total minus that minimum. 2.17
simple: Take exactly k cards from the two ends of a row. Maximise the total.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each i from 0 to k (cards from the front), sum the first i and the last k - i cards directly.
Keep the max.
approaches.why: k + 1 splits, each summed in O(k).
approaches.simple: Try every split (i from the front, k−i from the back) and add them up from scratch.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: sum = first k cards; best = sum.
For i from 1 to k: remove front card k - i, add back card n - i. Update best.
approaches.why: One pass to build the first window, then k O(1) slides.
approaches.simple: Start with the first k cards. Then swap one front card for one back card at a time, updating the sum.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
pattern: Variable sliding window (at most k bad elements)
problem: Given a binary array nums and an integer k, return the maximum number of consecutive 1s you can get if you may flip at most k zeros to ones.
example: Explanation: Flip the zeros at indices 5 and 10: [1,1,1,0,0,1,1,1,1,1,1]; the run from index 5 to 10 has
intuition: Rephrase: find the longest subarray containing at most k zeros. That is exactly the variable window template. Expand right; if it is a 0, zeros++. While zeros > k, move left forward (if nums[left] was 0, zeros--). Every valid window gives right - left + 1.
Like 2.12, there is a "non-shrinking window" variant: use if instead of while, so the window size never decreases. The final right - left + 1 is the answer. Both are O(n).
notes: Say it like this: "This is the longest subarray with at most k zeros. Brute force checks every start in O(n²). A sliding window that shrinks while zeros exceed k gives O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: k = 0 (longest run of 1s); k >= number of zeros (whole array); all zeros.
Common mistakes: decrementing zeros without checking that the element leaving is actually a 0.
Follow-ups: "Stream of bits, k = 1?" Track the index of the last zero; when you see a new zero, move left to lastZero + 1. Longest Substring With 2.18
simple: You may flip up to k zeros to ones. What is the longest run of ones?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i, extend j counting zeros.
Stop when zeros exceed k; track the longest valid length.
approaches.why: Each start can extend up to n.
approaches.simple: From each start, grow while the number of zeros stays at most k.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: left = 0, zeros = 0.
For each right: if nums[right] == 0, zeros++.
While zeros > k: if nums[left] == 0, zeros--; left++.
best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.why: left and right each move at most n times.
approaches.simple: Sliding window that counts zeros inside. Too many zeros? Move the left edge right until it is fine again.

title: Longest Substring With At Most K Distinct Characters
problem: Given a string s and an integer k, return the length of the longest substring that contains at most k distinct characters.
example: Explanation: "ece" has 2 distinct characters and length 3; no longer substring has at most 2 distinct.
intuition: Window is valid while the number of distinct characters is <= k. Keep a frequency map of the window; its size is the distinct count. Expand right, add the char. While map.size() > k, decrement s[left] and remove it from the map when its count hits 0, then left++. Record the length.
This is the general version of "Fruit Into Baskets" (k = 2).
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force extends from every start while tracking distinct characters, O(n²). A sliding window with a frequency map, shrinking while the map has more than k keys, gives O(n) time and O(k) space."
Edge cases: k = 0 (answer 0, the window always shrinks to empty); k >= distinct count of s (whole string); empty string.
Common mistakes: not removing keys with count 0 (map size stays wrong); using Map.size as a method in JS (it is a property).
Follow-ups: "Exactly k distinct, count substrings?" Use atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) (Subarrays with K Different Integers, LeetCode 992). "Fruit Into Baskets?" This with k = 2. Number of Substrings 2.19
simple: Find the longest stretch of text that uses at most k different letters.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each start i, extend j while adding characters to a set.
If the set size exceeds k, break; otherwise update best.
approaches.why: n starts, each extends up to n; the set holds at most k + 1 characters.
approaches.simple: From each start, grow while the set of letters stays at size k or less.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Map freq, left = 0.
For each right: freq[s[right]]++.
While freq.size() > k: decrement freq[s[left]], remove it if 0, left++.
best = max(best, right - left + 1).
approaches.why: Each character enters and leaves the window once; the map holds at most k + 1 keys.
approaches.simple: Sliding window with a letter count map. When the map has more than k letters, shrink from the left.

title: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters
problem: Given a string s of only 'a', 'b' and 'c', return the number of substrings that contain at least one occurrence of each of the three characters.
example: Explanation: Substrings with a, b and c: "abc", "abca", "abcab", "abcabc", "bca", "bcab", "bcabc", "cab",
intuition: "At least" counting has a nice property: if s[i..j] contains all three, every longer substring s[i..j'] with j' > j also does. So fix the end right instead, and ask: how many starts give a valid substring? A start i is valid if the window s[i..right] still contains all three, which means i <= min(last[a], last[b], last[c]). So the number of valid substrings ending at right is min(lastA, lastB, lastC) + 1.
Trace "abcabc": right=2 → last = {0,1,2}, min 0 → +1. right=3 → {3,1,2} min 1 → +2. right=4 → {3,4,2} → +3. right=5 → {3,4,5} → +4. Total 10.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force fixes each start and, once all three letters appear, counts every extension at once, O(n²). Fixing the end instead, the valid starts are exactly 0 through the minimum last-seen index of a, b and c, so I add min + 1 per position: O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: a letter missing entirely (answer 0); length < 3; "aaacb" style where all three appear only at the end.
Common mistakes: counting each valid window once instead of counting all its extensions; overflow is not an issue here for n ≤ 5·10⁴, but for larger n use long.
Follow-ups: "Do it with the classic shrinking window?" Expand right; while the window has all three, add n - right and shrink left. Same O(n). 2.20
simple: Count the pieces of the string that contain at least one a, one b and one c.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each start i, extend j, mark seen characters.
As soon as all three are seen, every extension also counts: add n - j and break.
approaches.why: Each start may extend up to n before seeing all three.
approaches.simple: From each start, grow until all three letters are seen; every longer piece also counts.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: last = [-1, -1, -1] for a, b, c.
For each right, set last[s[right]] = right.
Add min(last) + 1 to the answer (it is 0 while some letter has not appeared, since min is -1).
approaches.why: One pass, three integers.
approaches.simple: Remember the last position of a, b and c. For each right end, the smallest of those three positions tells how many start points work.

title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
pattern: Prefix sum + hash map / atMost(goal) - atMost(goal - 1)
problem: Given a binary array nums and an integer goal, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum equals goal.
intuition: "Exactly" is awkward for a sliding window: when the sum equals goal, adding a 0 keeps it equal, so we do not know whether to expand or shrink. "At most" is easy: for each right, shrink while the sum exceeds the limit, then every start from left to right is valid, so add right - left + 1. Then exactly(goal) = atMost(goal) - atMost(goal - 1).

Another general method is prefix sums: a subarray (i, j] has sum goal when prefix[j] - prefix[i] == goal. Count prefix values seen so far in a map and look up prefix - goal. That uses O(n) space; the window trick is O(1) space because all numbers are non-negative.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force enumerates subarrays, O(n²). Prefix sums with a hash map count subarrays with sum goal in O(n) time and O(n) space. Because the array is binary (non-negative), I can count 'at most goal' with a sliding window and subtract 'at most goal minus 1', which is O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: goal = 0 (count zero-runs: atMost(-1) must return 0); all zeros; goal larger than total ones (0).
Common mistakes: trying a single "exactly" window (misses subarrays with leading zeros); forgetting the g < 0 guard (the while loop would run past the end).
Follow-ups: "Negative numbers allowed?" Window breaks (sum is not monotonic); use the prefix-sum map (Subarray Sum Equals K, LeetCode 560). 2.21
simple: Count stretches of a 0/1 list whose sum equals goal.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each start i, extend j, keep a running sum.
Count when it equals goal; break once it exceeds goal (values are non-negative).
approaches.why: All subarrays in the worst case (e.g. all zeros).
approaches.simple: Try every start and grow while summing.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Map prefixCount with {0: 1}; running sum = 0.
For each element: sum += x; add prefixCount[sum - goal]; then increment prefixCount[sum].
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) map operations; the map can hold up to n + 1 prefix values. (This is the general method, it also works with negatives.)
approaches.simple: Prefix sums with a map, exactly like counting subarrays with sum k.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Write atMost(g): if g < 0 return 0. Sliding window: add nums[right]; while sum > g, subtract nums[left++]; add right - left + 1.
Return atMost(goal) - atMost(goal - 1).
approaches.why: Two linear window passes; only a few counters.
approaches.simple: Count windows with sum at most goal, minus those with sum at most goal − 1. The difference is exactly goal.

title: Count number of Nice subarrays
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, a subarray is "nice" if it contains exactly k odd numbers. Return the number of nice subarrays.
example: Explanation: The nice subarrays are [1, 1, 2, 1] and [1, 2, 1, 1].
intuition: Map each number to 1 if odd and 0 if even. Now the question is "count subarrays with sum exactly k" on a binary array, which is exactly 2.20. So reuse the same two tools: prefix counts with a map, or atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1) with a sliding window that counts odd numbers.
notes: Say it like this: "If I turn odd numbers into 1 and even into 0, this is 'count subarrays with sum exactly k'. Brute force is O(n²). Prefix counts give O(n) time and O(n) space. Since the transformed array is non-negative, atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1) with a sliding window gives O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: no odd numbers (answer 0 for k ≥ 1); k larger than the number of odds (0); all odd.
Common mistakes: using x % 2 == 1 in Java for odd check (fails for negatives, since -3 % 2 == -1); forgetting that "exactly" cannot be done by one plain window.
Follow-ups: "Another O(1) space trick?" Count even numbers before and after each block of k odds: for each block, add (evensBefore + 1) * (evensAfter + 1).
simple: Count stretches that contain exactly k odd numbers.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each start i, extend j and count odd numbers.
Count when it equals k; break when it exceeds k.
approaches.why: All subarrays in the worst case (e.g. all even numbers).
approaches.simple: Try every start and grow while counting odd numbers.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Array cnt where cnt[p] = number of prefixes with p odd numbers; cnt[0] = 1.
For each element: odd += x & 1; if odd >= k, add cnt[odd - k]; then cnt[odd]++.
approaches.why: One pass; the count array has n + 1 slots.
approaches.simple: Count prefixes by how many odd numbers they contain and look up the earlier count that differs by k.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: atMost(g): sliding window counting odd numbers; while odd > g, remove nums[left++]; add right - left + 1.
Return atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1).
approaches.why: Two linear passes, constant extra variables.
approaches.simple: At most k odd numbers minus at most k − 1, each counted with a sliding window.
